summary: Describes a private SIP header called P-Answer-State, used by the Open Mobile Alliance for Push to talk over Cellular. It indicates the answering mode of the handset and is meant only for that application. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A tiny label on a walkie-talkie style call that says whether the phone will pick up by itself or wait for the person.

subtitle: A private SIP header that lets push-to-talk servers say a handset will probably answer by itself, so the caller can start talking sooner.

tldr.problem: In Push to talk over Cellular, the caller must be able to speak almost as soon as the button is pressed, but waiting for the called handset to answer, even automatically, adds delay.
tldr.mechanism: A PTT Server that has reason to think the called handset is in Automatic Answer mode adds a P-Answer-State header with the value Unconfirmed to a SIP response. Another PTT Server can then answer the caller and buffer the caller's media until a response marked Confirmed arrives.
tldr.outcome: The header is a private extension for the OMA PoC application only, and the RFC says it is generally not applicable to the Internet as a whole. It is Informational and has since been updated.

today: RFC 4964 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 8996. The RFC itself limits the header to the OMA PoC application.

sections.title: Push to Talk and Why Speed Matters
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) is specifying Push to talk over Cellular (PoC), a service where SIP sets up half-duplex media sessions between participants, usually after a user pushes a button. This RFC describes a private SIP extension for PoC and says it may not be applicable to the general Internet.

OMA's requirements are stringent: the time from the button press to the indication to speak must be minimized. The RFC states that the extension makes assumptions about network topology and transitive trust, and that these assumptions are generally NOT APPLICABLE in the Internet as a whole.
sections.plainLanguage: When you press the button on a walkie-talkie, you want to talk right away, not wait around. This note helps make that wait shorter, but only on special phone networks.

sections.title: Answer Modes, PTT Servers and Indications
sections.content:
A PoC terminal can be set to Automatic Answer mode, where it accepts an invitation and plays media at once, or Manual Answer mode, where it alerts the user, who must accept first. A user may change the mode often.

A PTT Server is a SIP network server that does the network-side work for the service. It can act as a SIP proxy or as a back-to-back user agent (B2BUA). The RFC introduces four terms:

  • Unconfirmed Indication: the target has not been contacted yet, but an intermediate node has a hint that it will probably answer.
  • Unconfirmed Response: a SIP 18x or 2xx response carrying an Unconfirmed Indication.
  • Confirmed Indication: the target accepted the invitation and is ready to receive media.
  • Confirmed Response: a SIP 200 (OK) response carrying a Confirmed Indication.

Because bursts of speech are short, typically 10-30 seconds, the RFC says the extra end-to-end latency from buffering can be tolerated.
sections.plainLanguage: Your friend's phone can be set to 'pick up by itself' or 'ring and wait for me'. The helpers in the middle sometimes know which one it is, and can say 'probably yes' before the phone actually answers.

sections.title: How the Header Is Used
sections.content:
The P-Answer-State header can appear in a SIP 18x or 2xx response to an INVITE, typically a 183 Session Progress or a 200 (OK). It can also appear in the sipfrag of a SIP NOTIFY sent because of a SIP REFER. It has two values. Unconfirmed means the sender has a hint that the final destination will automatically accept, but it might still alert the user or refuse. Confirmed means the destination has accepted and is ready for media, and it is only allowed in a 200 (OK).

In the main flow, a PTT Server that is forwarding an INVITE and knows the called handset is probably in Automatic Answer mode sends a 183 with Unconfirmed. A PTT Server upstream that wants to buffer absorbs it and sends the caller a 200 (OK) with an answer. When the called handset really answers, the server that sent the Unconfirmed response adds Confirmed to the 200 (OK), the buffering server absorbs it, and it plays out the buffered media.

Receivers must treat a 200 (OK) without the header as a Confirmed Response. A 18x response without the header SHOULD NOT be treated as Unconfirmed, and a 18x carrying Confirmed MUST NOT be treated as Confirmed because that is invalid. A buffering server SHOULD release the session if no Confirmed Response arrives before its buffer overflows. Multiple PTT Servers are not meant to buffer serially.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper says 'probably going to answer', another helper catches your words in a bucket and tells you to go ahead. When your friend really answers, the bucket is emptied to them.

sections.title: Syntax and Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
The header is defined in ABNF as P-Answer-State followed by an answer type and optional generic parameters. The answer type is Confirmed, Unconfirmed or a generic token.

Ordinary SIP proxies do not need to understand the header, because SIP rules say proxies forward unknown headers. No Supported or Require header is needed, since the sender does not depend on the receiver understanding the extension; an unrecognized header is ignored. A PTT Server acting as a proxy MAY add Unconfirmed to a 18x it originates, or Confirmed to a Confirmed Response.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is just one word, 'Confirmed' or 'Unconfirmed'. Helpers who do not understand it simply pass it along and nothing breaks.

sections.title: Alternatives That Were Rejected
sections.content:
The RFC lists four other ways to carry the same hint and why each was dropped:

  • A special reason phrase in the 183 and 200 responses: reason phrases are meant for human readers, not for servers to parse.
  • A Reason header: this would be inconsistent with its intended use, is not defined for these response codes, and would need a new protocol identifier.
  • A feature tag in the Contact header: the answer state is an attribute of the session, not a separate feature.
  • A new SDP attribute: the answer state applies to the session and not to one media stream.

A new header was chosen so the caller can tell whether the invited subscriber or just an intermediary accepted the INVITE.
sections.plainLanguage: They thought about writing the note in other places, but each one was the wrong spot, like writing a message on the envelope when it belongs on a card inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not regard the header's contents as particularly sensitive, and says an eavesdropper gains nothing useful from it. End-to-end protection is not appropriate because proxies and intermediate user agents add and use the header.

A malicious proxy or an attacker on the signaling path could add, remove or change the header. The worse case is falsely signaling that the callee has not been contacted when they have already answered, which might make the caller decide not to send media. Implementations SHOULD use a transport that gives integrity and confidentiality between signaling hops, and TLS-based SIP signaling can do this. Security was only considered for trusted networks with hop-by-hop security and transitive trust, and use in the general Internet was not evaluated.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sneaky in the middle could change the note and trick the caller. So the helpers should pass notes through locked tubes.

viz.caption: SIMPLIFIED FROM THE RFC'S OVERVIEW OF THE FLOW

messages.label: 183 + Unconfirmed
messages.note: Hint that the callee will probably auto-answer.

messages.label: 200 (OK) with answer
messages.note: Caller starts sending media, which is buffered.

messages.label: 200 (OK) + Confirmed
messages.note: Buffered media is now played out.

data.title: ABNF
data.code:
P-Answer-State = "P-Answer-State" HCOLON answer-type
                 *(SEMI generic-param)
answer-type = "Confirmed" / "Unconfirmed" / token
